title: AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’
full_text: Sep 9, 2026 6:35am PT AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’ By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Suno Tries to Break Into Music Mainstream With New Label-Backed Model ‘v6’ 5 hours ago Suno Kills Controversial Mary J. Blige Ad Where She Seems to Endorse the AI Music Generator (EXCLUSIVE) 6 days ago AI Giant Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9 Billion 6 days ago See All Getty Images for HubSpot Multiple current and former Anthropic employees warned — and admitted — on Tuesday that the researchers building new AI models believe the technology could lead to humanity’s destruction by the end of the decade, reflecting the industry’s frenzy over reining in rapid development. Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, wrote on X that he resigned from the company on Tuesday because he believed the Dario Amodei-led company and OpenAI , his former employer, were “gambling with our lives” in how they improved the technology. Related Stories Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in 'An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,' Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE) ‘September 5’ Director Tim Fehlbaum Working on a ‘Historical Film’ Set in Berlin as Swiss Filmmakers Take on Challenges and Opportunities of Shooting in English “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote. “This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Popular on Variety Anthropic did not respond to an immediate request for comment, but Coxon’s warnings were surprisingly affirmed by Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment scene lead, and Samuel Marks, who runs the company‘s scalable oversight division. Hubinger wrote the company did “earnestly believe AI could kill all humans” and that he thought it was a greater than 10% risk “within the next desk.” “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote on X. Marks’ own X post , which he said he wrote in his personal capacity, said that AI researchers continue building the technology despite the risk of “human extinction” because of a financial incentive and the fear the technology would be developed by AI developers who may abuse its capabilities. “Many AI developer staff desperately want to slow down to figure out how to build AI more safely,” he wrote. “I work on safety research at Anthropic because I hope my work will reduce the chance of these extinction-level bad outcomes.” The comments from Anthropic employees reflect a broader public tonal shift among AI companies, many of which entered the market touting the transformative potential of AI models but now warn that those models risk escaping human control. Anthropic as a company has called for a development slowdown since June, while OpenAI paired its debut of GPT-6 Astra last week, which it claimed pushed the world into an era of artificial general intelligence, with several warnings by company leaders and researchers that a slowdown was needed to improve safety conditions. “No one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence,” wrote Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, in a blog post on Sunday that was later reposted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. Still, the industry sentiment has received pushback from the Trump administration, which has argued that slowing down development risks ceding the AI arms race to a rapidly evolving China. “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Breitbart on Tuesday. “Like everything, a trillion-and-a-half-dollar defense budget, the Iron Dome. title: Fox Says DOJ Taking Closer Look at Roku Megadeal
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 9, 2026 6:34am Fox Corp chief Lachlan Murdoch Drew Angerer/Getty Images The U.S. Department of Justice is taking a closer look at Fox Corp .’s $22 billion megadeal for Roku , the media company said Wednesday, potentially signaling regulatory scrutiny on a deal that would turn it into a digital video power player. In a securities filing Wednesday, Fox said: “On September 8, 2026, as expected, each of FOX and Roku received a request for additional information and documentary material (the ‘Second Request’) from the U.S. Department of Justice (the ‘DOJ’) in connection with the DOJ’s review of the Mergers.” “Issuance of the Second Request extends the waiting period under the HSR Act until 30 days after both FOX and Roku have substantially complied with the Second Request, unless the waiting period is terminated earlier by the DOJ or FOX and Roku otherwise agree to extend the waiting period,” the filing continued. “FOX and Roku will continue to work cooperatively with the DOJ in its review of the Mergers.” Fox says it still believes the deal is on track for a first half of 2027 close for the deal, which was announced in June. While the company says the second request was expected (indeed, they are not at all unusual for major deals), it nonetheless signals that there could yet be some regulatory scrutiny on the merger. It’s also hard to ignore the political elephant in the room: President Trump has frequently weighed in on major deals, and there has been a perception in the marketplace that companies with close ties to the White House are getting different treatment than companies perceived to be at odds with them. Paramount’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery, for example, was given the green light by the DOJ despite some staff attorneys expressing concern around the deal. In the case of Fox, while it may be seen as being closely allied with the White House, Fox News late last week said that it “parted ways” with Maria Bartiromo, sparking some anger from White House officials like Peter Navarro, and a post from President Trump commending her for her work there. But as the Paramount-WBD merger shows, with the deal now held up because of an antitrust suit brought by state AGs, any wrench in the process can become a major holdup to dealmaking. While the DOJ request may be standard for something of this size, it could portend a more challenging path forward than the companies originally anticipated. THR

title: Pablo Larraín’s ‘My Sad Dead’ Trailer: “The Dead Start To Make Themselves Present”
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart International Sales Of French TV Programs Crash To A Ten-Year Low Prime Video Gathers YA Stars For Alpine Retreat & Drops First Looks At ‘Boys of Tommen,’ ‘Our Fault: London’ & ‘Love Me Love Me 2’ Freya Allan & Kodi Smit-McPhee Star In Nick Hamm’s Jack The Ripper-Era Thriller ‘Black Palace’ — First Look View All September 9, 2026 6:32am EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Pablo Larraín’s Netflix miniseries My Sad Dead . Based on stories by acclaimed Argentine author Mariana Enriquez, the psychological horror will play in competition at the San Sebastian Film Festival later this month. Produced by Larraín’s Fabula, the much-anticipated series tells the story of Ema, a retired doctor grappling with grief after her mother’s death. She can see and speak with the dead around her, including her own mother. Mercedes Morán, Dolores Fonzi, Alejandra Flechner, and Carolina Álvarez star. Related Stories News Netflix South Africa Slate Includes Latest 'How To Ruin', 'Seriously Single' & 'Disaster Holiday' Editions News Netflix Orders 'Lonesome Dove' Series From Zoe Kazan & Jeb Stuart Based On Larry McMurtry's Novel Per the synopsis, the arrival of Ema’s niece, Julie, and the murder of three local teenagers trigger a strange phenomenon that breaks the fragile balance between the living and the dead. What had been Ema’s burden then begins to spread throughout the neighborhood: the dead start to make themselves present, and no one will be able to escape the sound of their own ghosts. “Living can sometimes be a truly terrifying experience; reality can induce sheer panic. Everyday life holds moments of terror, a quiet, unshowy kind of terror, stemming from things that are constantly close to you and, for that very reason, can be the most dangerous,” Larraín said. “ My Sad Dead shows us a city, poverty, violence, and people and social classes that have been forgotten. There is abandonment, death, and love, but at its core, the terror lies in the everyday.” The miniseries will run to four parts. The cast is rounded out by Carlos Portaluppi, Germán de Silva, and Chilean actress Luz Jiménez. It drops on Netflix on September 24. title: The 50 Most Powerful TV Producers of 2026
full_text: × Skip to main content Illustrated by Neil Jamieson; Meriwether, lawrence: Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images. Brunson: Robin L Marshall/Getty Images. lee, rogen: Araya Doheny/Getty Images for SAG-AFTRA Foundation. Lindelof: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images. fey: Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images. Dippold: Unique Nicole/Getty Images. levy: Theo Wargo/Getty Images. coben: Kevin Winter/Getty Images. Sennott: Dia Dipasupil/WireImage. goddard: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images. goldberg: Michael Kovac/Getty Images for AFI. han: Amy Sussman/Getty Images. Antosca: John Nacion/WireImage. this spread: bay: Courtesy of apple tv. trouble: Carl Herse/apple tv. rhimes: Amy Sussman/Getty Images for Vanity Fair. Gilligan: Robin L Marshall/Getty Images. Ignore that deep, existential AI dread for a moment — “It’s the devil’s tool,” cautions Damon Lindelof — and you’ll find that showrunners actually do have plenty to feel good about these days. Original concepts are selling again ( Widow’s Bay ! Pluribus !). Commercial success with the old model is still possible (see: High Potential or The Pitt ). Young people are watching more than just MrBeast attempting not to die on camera: Just look at Prime Video’s YA triumvirate of The Summer I Turned Pretty , Off Campus and Sterling Point . Hell, a Canadian import with zero marketing and a whole lot of gay sex turned two unknown actors into The Beatles. TV is so back! And even as creatives brace for the Warner Bros.-Paramount merger as if the moon herself were barreling toward the Southland to incinerate us all, THR ‘s annual poll of the most powerful writer-producers in TV dives into all the good stuff like show envy, the trends they’re glad to see die and the execs who impress them the most. And, yeah, sure, AI is coming for all our jobs. But it hasn’t yet. So take a breath and take note of Michelle King’s advice for aspiring TV scribes who might one day join the ranks of this storied list: “None of the sensible professions — lawyer, engineer, doctor — are safe from AI either. So, you might as well become a writer.” METHODOLOGY THR selected the Most Powerful TV Producers from all writing producers with live-action scripted series that aired original episodes in the U.S. between August 2025 and August 2026. With acknowledgment that roles and duties can vary significantly from show to show, each entrant is judged relative to slates, deal size, ratings, value to platform and studio, cultural impact, awards and, pivotally, who can actually sell a show in this bizarre and uncertain climate. Lucia Aniello, Paul W. Downs and Jen Statsky This trio gets the last laugh, scoring a record 24 Emmy nominations — the most for any comedy in a single year — for the fifth and final season of HBO Max’s Hacks . The Jean Smart juggernaut has made Aniello, Downs and Statsky among the most sought-after creatives in Hollywood. As for power? They shut down the damn Louvre to film their series finale. All three are under relatively fresh overall deals with Warner Bros., where they’re prepping a new HBO series, now that their long-running day job has finally come to an end. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Aniello “Loonen sparkling water by the case.” Downs “Verve Buena Vista coffee beans.” Statsky “Popcorn with Sour Patch Kids pre-mixed in.” 2026 series I’ve most admired Aniello “ A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms .” Downs “ Neighbors .” Statsky “ DTF St. Louis .” Lucia Aniello, Jen Statsky and Paul W. Downs Nick Antosca Long a genre king, the Channel Zero creator really stretched his muscles this year — delivering Apple TV a watercooler breakout (and approval from fellow EPs Steven Spielberg and Martin Scorsese) with his starry spin on Cape Fear . His Eat the Cat shingle also produced Murdaugh: Death in the Family for Hulu, while his next writing showcase is the high-stakes adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s Verity, starring Anne Hathaway. 2026 series I’ve most admired “There’s a ton I haven’t seen yet, but I’m loving Sterling Point .” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “Spindrift ginger ale and Aris mango greek yogurt.” Greg Berlanti After a surprisingly quiet stretch for one of Hollywood’s most dependably prolific showrunners, Berlanti is ramping up his TV efforts once more. As the clock finally runs out on the CW football drama All American , there have been series orders for Prime Video horror drama Stillwater and Netflix’s live-action Scooby Doo: Origins ; development with Disney+’s Afterlife With Archie and Netflix’s Nanny Diaries ; and, perhaps most auspiciously, a stacked drama pilot (Ray Romano, Joshua Jackson, Kaley Cuoco, Rita Wilson) hoping to replicate The Pitt ’s model at HBO Max. My advice for any baby writer “Be the most enthusiastic person in the room on a staff. If you haven’t staffed yet, write as much possible. That is more important than any connection you’ll make.” The scariest part about the TV business today “It’s not set up to raise and give the right amount of experience to a young/new generation of showrunners.” Quinta Brunson, Justin Halpern and Patrick Schumacker As Abbott Elementary hits its sixth season on ABC, we are getting a sense of what’s next for its creator-star after news that she would develop and star in a Betty Boop feature. Meanwhile, Halpern and Schumacker, the longtime co-showrunners of the Emmy-winning series that’s often credited with saving sitcoms, have a next act in place, too; they’re working with Bill Lawrence on I Suck at Girls , a comedy that nabbed a series order from Netflix in January. 2026 series I’ve most admired Brunson “ Furious ” A song I love and just can’t clear Halpern “I can’t remember ever successfully clearing a song we wanted that we could actually afford.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Schumacker “A personal chef. Crafty is a waistline killer.” Debora Cahn Overwhelmingly voted the most admired showrunner on our 2025 list, Cahn continues to do what most consider impossible these days: delivering a new globe-trotting season of The Diplomat on time, every fall — each one of which lands atop Netflix’s Top 10 chart and Emmy voters’ ballots. The third season is now up for seven Emmys, including outstanding drama. Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “Six commercial breaks in an hour.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Meryl Streep.” Courtesy Joanna Calo and Christopher Storer The Bear recently went into hibernation, presumably forever, but the duo that delivered all five seasons to FX on Hulu already have their next meals planned. Calo is one of at least two people on this list penning Marvel’s X-Men feature, and Storer, who created the onetime Emmy force, is producing pal Ramy Youssef’s feature directorial debut Martha & Muhammad . Harlan Coben When Coben isn’t collaborating with Reese Witherspoon on a novel or potentially IDing the Zodiac killer on his hit podcast, he’s selling more series than potentially any author since Agatha Christie. In the past 10 months, he’s delivered I Will Find You , a Netflix colossus viewed by 118 million to date, Run Away (also at Netflix), Prime Video’s Lazarus and the CBS true-crime effort Harlan Coben’s Final Twist — though something tells us he’s got more of those to come. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A shock collar that gives a sharp sting when anyone uses the words ‘synergy,’ ‘tonally,’ ‘elevate’ and mostly, ugh, ‘arc,’ as in story or character.” My advice for any baby writer “You can always fix bad pages. You can’t fix no pages.” The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Whoever greenlights my next project. That exec is clearly insightful, brilliant and very attractive.” Ryan Condal and Ira Parker It’s generally feast or famine with HBO’s Game of Thrones offerings, but throughout 2026 its fans ate. In January, Parker delivered critical smash Knight of the Seven Kingdoms with a producing assist from Condal. It got a renewal and an outstanding drama Emmy nom. Then, in June, House of the Dragon returned for its third and penultimate season with wild numbers (an average 34 million viewers to date) and a shockingly high body count. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Condal “I get to keep all the props.” Star I’m still dying to work with Parker “Jackie Chan.” My advice for any baby writer Condal “You cannot wait for success to come to you. Be an entrepreneur. Experiment in every medium: film, TV, comics, short fiction. You really do have to make your own success now more than ever.” Greg Daniels Daniels was once adamant that he’d never make any sort of reboot or companion to The Office , arguably the most successful comedy of the 21st century, but when he finally capitulated … at least he did a good job. The Paper , his pseudo-spinoff, dropped its first season on Peacock to 342 million viewing minutes last fall. It subsequently got a broadcast run on NBC. Critics have been even warmer with the sophomore season that debuts Sept. 9. Hey, that’s today! The scariest part about the TV business today “With so many writers making only 10 episodes a season, and a marketplace that feels more like book publishing with too many titles to sample, we might be past the era of the culturally unifying 120-plus-episode watercooler character comedies. More sad than scary.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A half hour of yard time after lunch and an Aeron chair.” Katie Dippold The world was not expecting a hilarious horror comedy to commandeer the cultural conversation at the tail end of spring, but that’s what Dippold delivered with Widow’s Bay . Overwhelmingly voted the favorite series of her peers on this list, the former Parks and Recreation and Ghostbusters writer’s first creation seemed to come from nowhere. And it’s not going away. Apple TV renewed it for a second season. Emmy voters lauded it with 19 noms. And Dippold finds herself atop many executives’ and actors’ lists of dream collaborators. Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “It seems that in both features and TV, we’re starting to see a little bit less ‘IP’ and a little bit more original work. As someone who has worked passionately on IP projects, I absolutely understand the appeal. But I think a greater balance is better for the industry.” My advice for any baby writer “When you’re stuck, try not to scroll the internet. Just let yourself sit in that boredom and daydream. The ideas will come. Also, make sure the first few pages of your writing samples are excellent. The unfortunate truth is that decision-makers — executives, producers, showrunners — get tons of samples. You aren’t guaranteed a full read. That doesn’t mean you should start with something gimmicky or attention-grabbing. Just aim for excellence, in whatever form, however that fits your voice.” Katie Dippold Rob Kim/Getty Images Matt and Ross Duffer Netflix and the Duffers’ plan to release the final season of seminal hit Stranger Things in three consecutive drops (Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day) worked better than anyone could have expected. The eight episodes quickly collected more than 134 million views. Producorial efforts The Boroughs and Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen were commercial and critical successes, but Netflix declined to renew both. Very odd, until you remember that the Duffers officially decamped in April for a rich five-year deal at Paramount … where expectations could not be higher. Song we love and just can’t clear The Duffer Brothers “Depeche Mode, anything of theirs from the ’80s.” Our advice for any baby writer The Duffer Brothers “It may sound trite, but don’t focus too much on what’s selling or what you see in the trades. Write what you love.” The star we’re still dying to work with The Duffer Brothers “Matt Damon” Julian Fellowes and Sonja Warfield Call it the little horse-drawn carriage that could. The Gilded Age , Fellowes and Warfield’s deliciously soapy period drama, has grown its audience consistently across the first three seasons — climbing another 30 percent in its last outing on HBO, which has it vying for best drama at the Emmys once again. No. 4 arrives in November when — spoiler? — we’ll finally find out if Carrie Coon is still dramatically staring out the window of Bertha’s Newport mansion. My advice for any baby writer Fellowes “Always write shows you want to see. Try guessing the likes and dislikes of a modern audience, and you will soon be in the soup. The truth is, people watch a show because they are interested in the characters, that is always true, and if you’re interested in the people you’re writing, then there’s a good chance the audience will be too.” 2026 series I’ve most admired Warfield “ America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders ” Tina Fey, Lang Fisher and Tracey Wigfield An experiment at more grounded comedy has been a success for this trio of 30 Rock scribes. The Four Seasons , their loose spin on Alan Alda and Carol Burnett’s movie of the same name, returned for a second season that spent weeks atop the Netflix Top 10, won over a few more critics and earned a renewal for season No. 3. Fey also produces The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins . The NBC sitcom, from other 30 Rock alums Robert Carlock and Sam Means, premiered as the most watched comedy telecast of the broadcast season. The TV executive who’s really impressed me … Fey “Jack Donaghy” My advice for any baby writer Fey “I probably wouldn’t give advice because the world they’re entering is so completely different the path I took. But I would pay for their lunch.” Fisher “Have many different samples. Half-hour, hour, comedy, drama, white wine thriller, etc.” Wigfield “Become a plastic surgeon instead. Or, if you want to be a comedy writer, make one funny TikTok a day. And maybe try to marry a plastic surgeon?” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Fisher “Must have warm jacket ready for her, because she will have forgotten for the one millionth time how cold the soundstage is and will be dressed for the beach.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Wigfield “I like how audiences are getting fed up with how much time can pass between seasons. I know it’s hard to make a show, but I’ve given birth to two children since the last season of Shogun .” Courtesy of Apple TV; John Nacion/WireImage Dan Fogelman and John Hoffman Together, Fogelman and Hoffman are wrapping up work on the sixth season of Hulu’s gift that keeps on giving. Only Murders in the Building , possibly the most star-studded series since Meryl Streep’s last show ( Big Little Lies ), just added five more Emmy noms to its tally. Fogelman is also up for an outstanding drama Emmy for Paradise , which returns in 2027 — around the time he launches the football drama The Land , also at Hulu. Song I love and just can’t clear Fogelman “I wanted to use ‘Anna Begins’ by The Counting Crows in This Is Us . Eventually, I was told the answer was no. While the band was happy to let us approve the usage, they needed ‘Mr. Jones’ to sign off and could not find him. I became fascinated by this morsel and may write a movie about it one day.” Hoffman “Oh, this is a sensitive one. It’s French and accompanies an intimate scene so perfectly and I’m right now still hoping it clears. I’ll take any and all vibes of support!” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Hoffman “A never-ending supply of Barebells Salty Peanut protein bars. Which will soon be revealed to be made by Snickers, I’m certain.” Erin Foster, Bruce Eric Kaplan and Jenni Konner If Nobody Wants This , why does this series keep winning over Netflix viewers and our cold, bitter hearts? Foster’s creation, co-showrun by comedy sherpas Kaplan and Konner, heads into its third season with a couple more Emmy noms. With sister Sara, Foster has a few other juicy titles (see: Hotter in the Hamptons ) in development as well. Konner has her side hustles too, recently showrunning the second and final season of Hulu’s Deli Boys . Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Foster “Male-dominated writers rooms.” The star I’m still dying to work with Foster “Sarah Pidgeon” Kaplan “David Harbour” Konner “I would kill to write for Julia Louis-Dreyfus.” Song I love and just can’t clear Konner “I’m not going to say this is a song I love, but I once tried to clear ‘Jump Around’ (which is seemingly in everything), and the band passed.” Megan Gallagher It is indeed All Her Fault , and Gallagher is probably happy to take the blame. Her Peacock limited series finally put the streamer on the map for original content. The “white wine thriller,” as the town has brilliantly dubbed the female-friendly genre, premiered as its most watched scripted original — logging 46 million hours viewed in the first four weeks. It also earned Gallagher an overall deal with Universal Global Television, where she’ll tackle another miniseries: The Break-In . But that’s after she launches The Blame on ITVX. Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “Vampires! They’re fun, but it’s time to move on.” A song I love and just can’t clear “‘And She Was’ by The Talking Heads.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Merritt Wever.” R. Scott Gemmill, John Wells and Noah Wyle In 2000, Saturday Night Live aired a sketch of Chris Parnell reading fawning reviews of The Sopranos aloud until he just sounded like he was having an orgasm. What does that have to do with these guys? Well, it’s basically how critics have responded to their platform-defining drama. The Pitt ’s second season bested high expectations by averaging north of 15 million viewers on HBO Max, netting another 25 Emmy nominations and sending almost everyone who writes about TV into a hyperbolic fervor that would make a Shaker blush. Its novel format, a prestige take on broadcast fare with an annual cadence and 15 episodes a season, is the envy of every executive, and now they’re all looking for a Pitt of their own. 2026 series I’ve most admired Gemmill “I was really impressed with how they brought Hacks to a close this year.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Wells “Romanticizing male serial killers.” Star I’m still dying to work with Gemmill “Hoping to work with Harrison Ford one day.” The scariest part about the TV business today Wells “Fewer and fewer buyers.” Vince Gilligan The undisputed king of prestige TV returned from his brief hiatus with an ultra-secretive, high-stakes drama that succeeded on every level. Pluribus premiered on Apple TV every bit as weird, hilarious and thought-provoking as one would expect from the brain behind Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul . It averaged a stunning 87 out of 100 on review aggregator Metacritic — this list does not have time for the simps at Rotten Tomatoes — and while Gilligan may claim he doesn’t have a long-term plan for his sci-fi Rhea Seehorn showcase, his track record shows that viewers are in good hands. My advice for any baby writer “Don’t ever, ever, ever, ever let AI do your job for you. Not a first draft, not a rewrite, not an outline, not even a riff session. If you do, your soul will be forfeit and you’ll burn in everlasting hellfire. Maybe that’s overstating it a tad, but you’ll sure as shit never work with me.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Charlize Theron. She’s cool. Also Carol Burnett, again.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “I really enjoyed The Audacity on AMC. Jonathan Glatzer is a good writer and a good guy. He used to work with us on Better Call Saul . Wherever he’s headed with his story, I’m along for the ride… but I hope to see those sociopathic tech bros of his get some major comeuppance in season two. And then, fingers crossed, may life imitate art.” Rhea Seehorn and Vince Gilligan at the world premiere of Pluribus in November 2025. Frazer Harrison/Getty Images Drew Goddard Many would be content just writing and producing one of the biggest films of the year: the $684 million-grossing Project Hail Mary , which united the globe in its love for an adorable rock alien who befriends Ryan Gosling. Not Goddard. He’s got a day job to think of, producing popular ABC procedural High Potential . The second season, which upped its episode count to 18, saw its average viewership climb past 16 million — making it one of the most watched linear shows out there. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “I appreciate that you think I don’t have a rider.” A song I love and just can’t clear “I’m genuinely excited when an artist won’t license their songs. My first thought is “Good for them!” Prince rules, is what I’m saying.” The scariest part about the TV business today “The growing number of people in positions of power who have zero interest in the art itself.” Evan Goldberg and Seth Rogen These two continue to kill it even when their Emmy-winning industry satire The Studio is absent from the metaphorical airwaves. In addition to unleashing another season of Apple TV’s Platonic , Goldberg and Rogen bid a bloody farewell to Prime Video’s The Boys and breathed new life into some of the trickiest IP to crack: The Muppets. Their Disney+ update of The Muppet Show pulled in nearly 8 million viewers. We’re as eager for a repeat performance as we are for The Studio to return and skewer this deeply unserious town. A song I love and just can’t clear Rogen “‘Simon Says’ by Pharoahe Monch because it has an illegal sample from the original Godzilla score.” 2026 series I’ve most admired Goldberg “ Widow’s Bay ! Katie Dippold absolutely nailed the tone. It’s hilarious, horrifying and just so well done.” Star I’m still dying to work with Rogen “I’m a huge fan of Jesse Eisenberg, and think I could write some funny stuff for him, but probably not as good as the stuff he writes for himself.” The TV executive who’s really impressed me … Goldberg “Michelle Lee. I don’t know how she puts up with all our crap and still supports us, but she does, and I’m very grateful for it.” Howard Gordon Industry vet Gordon is a rare breed of producer that could assemble a dream pairing ( Homeland collaborator Claire Danes and jack of all trades Matthew Rhys) for a limited series thriller so wholly original that it made most entries in that sprawling canon look like absolute schlock. No shade! The Beast in Me , created by Gabe Rotter, was a showcase for two TV icons who are each in the running for two of the series’ nine Emmy noms on Sept. 14. The scariest part about the TV business today “Once upon a time, series were platformed by designated ‘time slots,’ so a hit show became a kind of national campfire around which large sections of the country could gather to watch that week’s offering at the same time and on the same day. That time-dependency made it not only culturally impactful but highly profitable, things we so willingly traded for the convenience of streaming.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “ Half-Man was brilliant, uncomfortable, uncompromising and original.” Alfred Gough and Miles Millar Wednesday , Gough and Millar’s update of The Addams Family , is still the record holder for most watched English-language Netflix original by a mile. The first season has logged 252 million views, and season two fetched 119 million. That’s 2.65 billion hours viewed. Or 302,203 earth years of Wednesday watched. It’s also why its third season will anchor the dominant streamer’s 2027 release schedule as multiple spinoffs remain in play. The scariest part about the TV business today Gough and Millar “The system isn’t designed to train the next generation of showrunners and producers. We’re losing the apprenticeship that taught people how to actually make television.” Star we’re still dying to work with Gough and Millar “Tilda Swinton. We suspect she may actually be an Addams.” James Gunn, Tom King and Damon Lindelof and Chris Mundy After writing every episode of Peacemaker , Gunn, the head of DC Studios, entrusted his serial follow-up to a Justice League of three wildly different writers. Lanterns comes from Watchmen auteur Lindelof, Ozark vet Mundy and comic book writer (and former CIA officer!?) King. The August premiere scored strong reviews and nearly 10 million viewers in just three days, likely leaving Marvel TV green with envy. Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Gunn “2.35 aspect ratio in TV shows. It’s pretentious. That’s not the shape of our TVs! It makes the shows smaller!” Lindelof “Dark, revisionist takes on previously fun IP. (Yeah, yeah, I know.)” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Lindelof “No shorts in the writers room!” King “I can bring my dog with me. Sure, she’s a 60-pound, poorly-behaved rescue pit who would ruin everything by barking, but that poor, sad face when I leave the house…” My advice for any baby writer King “Never use ‘I got this’ or ‘You got this’ in a climactic scene. Same with any form of ‘Watch your six’ in an action moment.” Mundy “Don’t try to guess what other people want to read or watch. Write what you’d like to see. The difference will show up on the page.” The scariest part about the TV business today Gunn “The future comes more quickly at you than it used to.” Mundy “Seasons are smaller numbers of episodes but take so much longer to make than they used to. Which allows for better quality control, so, great. But the flip side of that is it makes it harder for people trying to break into the business.” Courtesy of HBO Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns Jenny Han People talk a lot about “event television,” but rarely does it reach the level that Han engineered for the finale (sort of) for The Summer I Turned Pretty . A surprise Paris premiere last fall turned into a reveal for a film continuation for the hugely successful YA show, one that reached 70 million viewers in its third run on Prime Video. She may be focused on her TSITP feature, but her To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before extended universe continues to deliver for Netflix with spinoff XO, Kitty . Star I’m still dying to work with “So many! Colman Domingo is my favorite part of anything he is in. Saoirse Ronan is so real and human and wonderfully alive in every role. Amy Adams, I would go to war for. Greta Lee because she is the coolest, the funniest, the sharpest, and she makes everything better.” Noah Hawley FX and Hawley continue to have one of the stronger symbiotic relationships in Hollywood. The pair committed to a new deal at the end of 2025 as Hawley readies the second season of his ambitious IP swing Alien: Earth and preps his fourth series at the platform: Far Cry , an adaptation of the video game anthology he’s making with Rob McElhenney. (And is a return to Fargo too much to ask for?) Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “The ‘tortured antihero’ suffers so we can sleep soundly at night.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “Nothing that was inevitable should be treated like a crisis.” Brad Ingelsby An actual second season of Mare of Easttown may still be straddling the line between gossip and green light, but Pennsylvania’s favorite son remains invested in his dormant hit. He’s brought back one character (Julianne Nicholson’s Lori) for the second season of Task , which is expected in 2027. The first season, also starring Mark Ruffalo, ranks among HBO’s three fastest-growing series to date. The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Francesca Orsi. She has a brilliant storytelling mind, and she’s passionate and relentless when she believes in something. It’s very inspiring.” The scariest part about the TV business today “For me, it’s the long, demanding hours worked by crew members and making sure everyone gets home safe at the end of the night.” Mindy Kaling The Los Angeles Lakers may be in a spot of tumult, but their fictional counterparts on Kaling’s Netflix basketball comedy are doing just fine. Running Point scored a speedy third-season renewal. And while Hulu opted not to renew Not Suitable for Work , the prolific and highly sought-after Kaling will be back with other shows. And more shows after that. She’s one of the last writer-producers in Hollywood who can truly sell to anyone, in any climate. The scariest part about the TV business today “A really long, deeply personal out-of-office reply.” The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Every executive I’ve ever worked with is a genius and gives perfect notes.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “I love Shark Tank .” Mindy Kaling David E. Kelley Plenty of actors would commit a federal crime to work with Kelley, a scribe of legend. His wife, Michelle Pfeiffer, chose to play the long game. And it paid off. Their first TV collaboration, Apple TV’s Margo’s Got Money Troubles , topped the streamer’s proprietary charts and earned them both Emmy nominations. Up next, Kelley has a second season of Margo and Presumed Innocent at Apple TV, along with Netflix’s adaptation of Harlan Coben’s Myron Bolitar novels. My advice for any baby writer “Read what you write aloud.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “The producer credit shall be earned.” A song I love and just can’t clear “‘Baby Can I Hold You’ by Tracy Chapman.” Courtney A. Kemp Kemp departed Netflix for Apple TV earlier in the year, but not before delivering a hit to the streamer she called home for four years. Drama Nemesis spent five weeks in the Top 10. It’s another point of validation for Kemp, whose series Power , in which she’s no longer creatively involved, continues to keep Starz afloat with spinoff No. 4, Origins , on deck next. My advice for any baby writer “Write and produce a small web series or a bunch of interconnected IG content. Get as many people to casually bump into your writing as possible. There are no barriers to reaching execs and showrunners now if you strike the right tone — their algorithms will do the work for you.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Angela Bassett or Viola Davis.” Michelle King and Robert King For any actor fretting over a move from Los Angeles to New York, just remember that’s where the Kings work. The husband-and-wife duo populate their projects with so many Broadway stars that the Law & Order casting director probably has pictures of them on a dartboard. On top of Elsbeth , a rare CBS and Paramount+ hit not made by Taylor Sheridan, the pair who brought us The Good Wife is about to launch another legal drama: Cupertino . Rest assured, it won’t be shooting in Silicon Valley. A song I love and just can’t clear Michelle King “ ‘Chitty Chitty Bang Bang,’ on more than one show, because we clearly live on the rock ’n’ roll edge.” 2026 series I’ve most admired Robert King “ Star City . An amazingly involving series that replaced every element of soap opera with spy thriller.” Michelle King “South Park” My advice for any baby writer Robert King “Never use AI in the development of key art.” Eric Kripke With his Prime Video behemoth’s May conclusion, The Boys became The Men . Some of them, at least. (Remind us which major characters even survived?) But worry not, fans of Kripke’s sly political commentary masquerading as comic book spoofs. He’s producing the upcoming prequel Vought Rising . 2026 series I’ve most admired “Everyone’s going to say Widow’s Bay , which is true, so I’m going to add Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man! for just how much he inspires me.” A song I love and just can’t clear “‘When the Levee Breaks’ by Led Zeppelin. I wanted it as the ending song for The Boys Season 4 finale. It was gonna be so good! Heartbreaker. (Which is also a hard-to-clear Zeppelin song.)” The scariest part about the TV business today “Not sending writers to set. We’re not training the next generation of show runners. Short sighted and dangerous for the future of the business.” Bill Lawrence Lawrence is prone to talk about his time in the TV penalty box, but it’s hard to reconcile that with his current reality. The power producer, who’s been working for Warner Bros. for some time now, has five current series on the air: HBO’s Rooster , ABC’s Scrubs reboot and Apple TV’s Shrinking , Bad Monkey and Ted Lasso . His involvement on all of them varies dramatically, but it’s worth noting that the one he’s most hands-on with, Shrinking , is also the one nominated for nine Emmys. 2026 series I’ve most admired “For me, it’s all about The Pitt . I can’t believe the high quality of work, the production value, how frenetic it feels. It’s super hard to make a medical show feel that visceral and real and still be over-the-top entertaining. I’ve tried.” The scariest part about the TV business today “Probably that it doesn’t feel like they’re making a ton of stuff. But I’m staying optimistic because I’ve been around long enough that I’ve seen the death of the comedy, the death of the drama, the death of the comedy again, reality TV is going to replace everything… and yet good stories keep coming out and grabbing people. So, I’m going to stick with content is king.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past “True crime. I’m joking because everything is true crime and it’s all my wife ever watches, but man, I’d like it to be over.” Bill Lawrence at his office on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. Photographed by Roger Kisby Lee Sung Jin Where’s the Beef ? Likely on most of the top 10 lists you’ll be reading when 2026 comes to a close. Lee’s follow-up to his lauded 2023 anthology upped the star power (Youn Yuh-jung!) and delivered on incredibly high expectations. Publicly, he’s been noncommittal about the future of the Netflix franchise — up for another 16 Emmys. But he’s got other things going, like working on the script for the X-Men movie that had every actor under the age of 30 war-calling their agent. The scariest part about the TV business today “The industry made almost 50 percent fewer shows this year. Meanwhile, more and more writers rooms have become a room of one. That being said, there will always be a need for storytelling, and I’m hopeful there will be healthier cycles somehow on the horizon, much like the movie business this year.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Tied between Tom Cruise and Cate Blanchett.” My advice for any baby writer “Be yourself while perfecting your craft. Having a point of view is the most important, as you are the rare 1 in 8 billion commodity, but it will go further if you spend time perfecting your craft on the technical side.” Louisa Levy For anyone who hadn’t heard of Levy’s work before May, that changed the minute her adaptation of the spicy YA hit Off Campus premiered as the third-most-watched debut in Prime Video history with 36 million viewers in less than two weeks. In lieu of a victory lap, Levy went right back to work. She’s already filming season two in Canada, which is great news for its rabid, albeit slightly creepy, parasocial fan economy. A song I love and just can’t clear “Hannah’s original karaoke song in season 1 was AC/DC’s ‘You Shook Me All Night Long”’ but we couldn’t get it! I’m not mad though. It opened the door for us to use Warrant’s “Cherry Pie.” The scariest part about the TV business today “How few jobs there are. It was tough to have such a big boom and then such a constriction. Especially in Los Angeles. So many talented folks are out of work.” My advice for any baby writer “Study the craft of writing but also learn how to participate in a room. Eighty percent of TV writing is talking, 20 percent is writing, and 50 percent is navigating relationships. How does that add up to 100 percent? Figuring out the math is producing.” Chuck Lorre The sitcom king is still turning out personalized vanity cards after every episode of every series he produces — of which there are currently three: CBS’ Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage , Netflix’s Leanne and HBO Max’s Stuart Fails to Save the Universe . He’s Chuck Lorre … what more do you want us to say? Seth MacFarlane MacFarlane might still make more money than you can fathom from his enduring animated hits Family Guy and American Dad! , but his live-action output is enviable, too. The folks at Peacock have got to be pleased with his comedy double header of The ’Burbs and Ted — and his coup in scoring the rights to the viral Dungeon Crawler Carl book series, potentially one of the most consequential TV deals done this year. Leon Bennett/Getty Images Liz Meriwether Just when you think you’ve got the New Girl creator showhorned — get it? — in sitcoms, she delivers an epic string of prestige hits ( The Dropout, Dying for Sex and, now, Hulu’s Furious ) and then signs on to write Jon M. Chu’s Britney Spears biopic. But Meriwether’s return to features isn’t full time. On top of ample development, the wildly versatile scribe just secured a second season of her Emmy Rossum collab. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A blanket. Always. I can’t write without a blanket covering at least half of my body.” Song I love and just can’t clear “I’m still sad that we couldn’t clear Tori Amos’ song ‘Little Earthquakes’ in the New Girl pilot. A good portion of my teenage years was spent blasting that cassette tape and driving around suburban Michigan thinking that no one understood my pain.” The scariest part about the TV business today “That streaming platforms are not making as much TV, which means that people aren’t taking as many chances. New voices are getting lost in the process. Writing and shooting a failed pilot was my way into producing my own writing at a large scale. It was how I got my sea legs, and I just don’t think new writers are getting that chance to try and fail and try again. New voices will always find a way to appear, but it’s increasingly not through television, which feels like a huge loss.” Ryan Murphy He may not always have the critics on his side, but nobody knows how to launch a show like Murphy. After giving the world the most unhinged press tour (Hulu’s All’s Fair ), he heralded FX’s The Shards with so many L.A. billboards that Kaia Gerber briefly outpaced the German shepherd from Veronica’s Insurance. The American Love Story producer simply knows how to get stuff on air and in people’s faces, which is why you can’t currently hide from the fact that his American Horror Story is back for lucky season No. 13. Jonathan Nolan, Geneva Robertson-Dworet Together, Nolan and Robertson-Dworet manage one of the most ambitious, expensive and, to everyone at Amazon’s relief, popular series going right now. The second season of Fallout reached more than 83 million pairs of eyeballs worldwide in its first 13 weeks of release. Season three is set to wrap production in September, hopefully freeing up star Walton Goggins to bank a few more Walmart commercials. Song we love and just can’t clear Nolan “‘Is That All There Is’ by Peggy Lee.” Robertson-Dworet “‘The Wanderer” by Dion. One of the best songs in the history of the Fallout games.” The scariest part about the TV business today Nolan “Fear of fear itself. The rumors of the industry’s demise are greatly exaggerated.” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Robertson-Dworet “Not disparaging any trend, but I’m personally glad Fallout doesn’t have an aftershow so I don’t have to be on it.” Megan Park, Stephanie Savage and Josh Schwartz What do you get when you combine the YA Midas touch of Savage and Schwartz with an ascendant filmmaker like Park? Arguably the series of the summer. It was a late entry for Sterling Point , but within two weeks of its Aug. 5 launch, Prime Video says it took in 36 million viewers. A sophomore season was quickly ordered, one Savage and Schwartz will work on when they’re not busy with their recently ordered Paramount+ update of Clueless . Star I’m still dying to work with Park “Sandra Bullock. She has always been my all-time favorite. I’m working on trying to make that one happen …” Trend I’m so glad to see the industry moving past Savage “Thinking that YA wasn’t a viable genre anymore …” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … Schwartz “More flights please! With so many shows shooting out of town, you end up spending months away from your family.” A song I love and just can’t clear Park “‘Sundown’ by Gordon Lightfoot. I have wanted to put it in everything I’ve made. It reminds me of my childhood summers in Canada.” Tyler Perry Extending his TV partnership with BET Media Group through 2028, the Atlanta-based producing giant is by no means limited to his many, many Paramount offerings. Netflix original Beauty in Black has proved so popular for the streamer, it recently reversed course and uncanceled the series with the announcement of a fourth season. In this economy? Shonda Rhimes The reigning monarch of Shondaland renewed her Netflix megadeal for a second time in August. This new five-year pact will keep her overseeing Bridgerton , the Regency drama that’s logged 610 million views since its 2023 bow to become one of the streamer’s defining hits. And while she may no longer be hands-on at ABC’s Grey’s Anatomy , it’s worth noting that her creation heads into season 23 as one of the most watched broadcast and streaming series. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “If? Girl, get you a team that fights for a rider.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “Pluribus.” The scariest part about the TV business today “AI is used to take jobs from hard-working craftspeople who work on sets. Also, the consolidation of studios will mean the narrowing of options for writers and producers. Devastating.” Star I’m still dying to work with “BEYONCÉ KNOWLES CARTER.” Mike Schur Known for his serial collaborations, Schur, who also executive produced Hacks , has two reunions of note in the queue. There’s a third season for Netflix’s Man on the Inside , starring his Good Place collaborator Ted Danson, and Peacock’s forthcoming Dig , a Parks and Recreation reteam with Amy Poehler. The latter drops all 10 episodes Thanksgiving week. A song I love and just can’t clear “’Ghost’ by Neutral Milk Hotel.” The scariest part about the TV business today “The scariest thing about the TV business is how scared everyone is about the TV business.” Rachel Sennott She may have co-created Big Mistakes with Dan Levy, but Sennott seems to make very few of her own. She spends her day-to-day creating and starring in her HBO comedy vehicle, I Love LA , which has been called Gen Z’s answer for Girls or S ex and the City . One could also call it a Gotham TV award winner and one of HBO’s fastest-growing comedies. 2026 series I’ve most admired “ Industry . Insane performances and incredible writing. And Dianna Agron just joined the cast for season five? I’m freaking out …” A song I love and just can’t clear “There’s a remix of the song ‘La Musique’ that I couldn’t get for season one. If anyone hears this, I’ll do anything please and thank you!” The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Amy Gravitt. She always picks up the phone and gives me the real immediately. We talk at like 5am all the time.” Rachel Sennott, creator and star of I Love LA . Kenny Laubbacher/HBO Taylor Sheridan Yeehaw! When he’s not minting new hit (CBS’ Marshals ) after hit (Paramount+’s Dutton Ranch ) after hit ( The Madison ) or tending to his ongoing series ( Lioness, Mayor of Kingstown, Tulsa King, Landman ) or writing his first book ( How to Not Die in Prison: A Survival Guide ), Sheridan is going on podcasts to talk about how much Hollywood doesn’t like him. Taylor, Universal just bet the farm on you with that landmark deal to swipe you from David Ellison. Hollywood likes you just fine. Charlotte Stoudt Stoudt is tasked with landing one of the biggest planes in streaming history with the upcoming conclusion of The Morning Show . Apple TV’s megawatt drama, starring Reese Witherspoon and Jennifer Aniston, wrapped filming on its fifth and final season this summer. That will air in 2027, when you could say it’ll return to the streamer’s Top 10 — but that would suggest it had fallen off it. The TV executive who’s really impressed me … “Dana Walden should ditch Disney and run for president.” 2026 series I’ve most admired “ Mr. Scorsese – a complex protagonist with an incredible story arc.” A song I love and just can’t clear “John Brion’s ‘Little Person’ from Synecdoche, New York . Devastating.” Jason Sudeikis What seemed highly unlikely just a few years ago became reality in August when Sudeikis unveiled the rebooted fourth season of his pandemic-defining Emmy winner Ted Lasso . The feel-good comedy, aided by new co-showrunner Jack Burditt, won back viewers who helped set an Apple TV record with 296.6 million minutes streamed in just two days. Believe, I guess? Jacob Tierney It’s hard to remember the last time a project so completely seized the pop culture discourse as Heated Rivalry did when the Canadian import got a U.S. run on HBO Max. Tierney, previously known for his work on Letterkenny and Shoresy , turned the quiet December drop into an 11 million viewer phenomenon that platformed gay narratives like never before and minted generational stars out of leads Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams. The star I’m still dying to work with | “I love Chris Evans. He’s an old-fashioned movie star, and I love movie stars.” The scariest part about the TV business today “That we are back in the time where there are only four or five places to take your shows to, and, if they don’t want them, you’re kind of out of options.” If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “A good napping situation, instead of falling asleep in a chair I find on set that I’m not supposed to be in. Someone is always telling me that if I sit in a chair that says ‘please do not sit,’ then everyone else will think they can sit in it.” Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in Heated Rivalry . Crave/Bell Media Jonathan Tropper The list is almost over, so you know how much it pained us to wait this long to describe someone as having “a banner year.” Well, it was worth the wait. Because what a nice run Tropper is enjoying. The novelist and filmmaker has seen his Jon Hamm vehicle Your Friends & Neighbors become a prototype for a serial streaming drama — and it finally broke into the Emmy race. Tropper also ran Lucky , the Apple TV thriller from Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine. As for 2027, there’s just the small matter of his friggin’ Star Wars: Starfighter screenplay. If producers had riders, the first thing on mine would be … “Don’t let me drive. I will be on the phone, and I will crash.” Star I’m still dying to work with “Scarlett Johansson.” Dick Wolf At 79, Wolf has five series on NBC ( Law & Order, Law & Order: SVU and his trio of Chicago dramas), two series on CBS ( FBI and CIA ) and, in our dreams, nightly calls to gossip with Mariska Hargitay. He is a titan. He is a TV legend. And, just saying, he probably has the sway to get most platforms to pony up for a series to be shot in Los Angeles. We have cops and courtrooms, too, Dick! This story appeared in the Sept. 9 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: The Athlete Is the Studio
full_text: × Skip to main content By Justin Birnbaum, Sportico Plus Icon Justin Birnbaum, Sportico View All September 9, 2026 6:30am LÆMEUR Coco Gauff has something to confess: She’s been nervous. But the 22-year-old tennis phenom, speaking over the phone after an early August training session, isn’t referring to the National Bank Open in Toronto, where in a few days she would begin a run to the semifinal. Nor is she talking about the U.S. Open at the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, a tournament that will eventually pit her against Mirra Andreeva in a highly anticipated quarterfinal matchup on Wednesday, Sept. 9. In 2025, Gauff launched a production company called iROC Media Group and shortly thereafter partnered with Religion of Sports , the Los Angeles-based studio founded by Tom Brady, Michael Strahan and Gotham Chopra, to produce a range of projects. The joint venture a few weeks ago released its first original offering: a pair of shortform documentaries for the Tennis Channel covering the history of fashion in the sport and the story of Zina Garrison, the first Black woman to reach a Grand Slam singles final in the Open era. Related Stories THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue The $100 Billion Race to Build the World's Next Sports Mecca THR + Sportico: The Sports Issue Esports Was Supposed to Be Bigger Than the NBA. What Happened? The addition of “executive producer” to Gauff’s résumé — alongside two-time Grand Slam singles champion, U.S. flag-bearer at the 2024 Paris Olympics and the youngest player to ever qualify for the Wimbledon main draw at just 15 years old — has caused some jitters. “I didn’t know how people would perceive it, to be honest,” she says. “But a lot of people were excited about it, and, obviously, I have to wait for feedback in September. That’s the hardest thing.” There are plenty of sports stars who can relate. Over the course of the past two decades, some of the most popular athletes on the planet have established similar businesses to service their creative ambitions, spanning documentaries, TV shows, feature films, podcasts and across multiple genres. (C) Jayden Daniels in Quarterback : Season 3. Courtesy of Netflix LeBron James co-founded the earliest form of the SpringHill Co. in 2007, which has since merged into Fulwell Entertainment. Stephen Curry helped create Unanimous Media in 2018, and Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions emerged two years later. A 2025 study by USC Annenberg’s Norman Lear Center identified 33 athlete-owned production companies that have generated more than 370 media properties, led by other notable names like Naomi Osaka, Kevin Durant and Tony Hawk. More recently, Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen entered the fold last week by launching Out of Pocket Studios with Skydance Sports. What all these enterprises have in common is that they’re underpinned by a desire for more control. The modern athlete wants a larger say in how they’re perceived, how their intellectual property is used and how they’re compensated. That’s exactly what Gauff, the world’s highest-paid female athlete at $31 million in 2025 , was after when last year she formed a namesake company to house all her business ventures in partnership with powerhouse agency WME, with the media business underneath. “I don’t want to just promote a brand or a product,” she says. “I really want to be a part of it.” It’s also how James, the first active NBA player to achieve billionaire status , framed some of his own moves. “I got sick and tired of the media changing the narrative or picking their narrative about what I was doing,” he said in a 2022 Sports Illustrated cover story. Endeavoring to build a media empire is easier said than done, though. Many of these upstarts have historically been quick to parlay a buzzy name and big bankroll into an initial slate of projects, generally centered around its athlete founder. Giannis Antetokounmpo, for example, rolled out Improbable Media in 2024 with a feature-length documentary about his life story. And, for a time, that would be enough to get a business off and running, especially with the demand for sports-related content booming. Hollywood has changed. The fallout of the COVID-19 shutdowns and the concurrent writer and actors strikes of 2023 has left an indelible mark on the entertainment industry. Studios have shrunk budgets, major production houses have cut staff, and fewer projects are reaching the finish line. That’s not to say there isn’t opportunity — Netflix and Amazon spent about $40 billion combined on video and music content last year — but the degree of difficulty, especially for the sports stars dabbling in unfamiliar territory, has intensified. “Any athlete can walk a project in and have it sell, quote unquote,” says Josh Pyatt, the former co-head of WME Sports who joined Patrick Whitesell’s investment firm WTSL as a partner earlier this year and now runs WIN Artists, its media, content and brand partnerships division. “Getting it made, getting multiple projects made and creating real enterprise value is something that not many can actually do.” (L to R) Kauchani Bratt as Jimmy, River Rayne Thomas as Tyson and Jojo Jackson as Warlance in Rez Ball. Lewis Jacobs/Netflix LESSONS FROM KING JAMES Gauff can’t take credit for the idea to push into the media business. That belongs with her father, Corey. In 2020, amid the COVID quarantine and the absence of sports, the elder Gauff was inspired by watching The Last Dance , an eight-part docuseries that chronicled Michael Jordan’s legendary career. He thought it would be cool to one day produce something similar about his then-16-year-old daughter if she could continue to win in the years to come. Gauff agreed, even though to this day, she still hasn’t seen the documentary. “It’s really bad that I haven’t watched yet,” Gauff says with a laugh. The irony is that while Jordan never founded his own media and production company, some industry insiders suggest that it’s hard not to see his imprint on this era. The basketball legend’s first Nike deal, which landed him a royalty on the sale of every sneaker bearing his name, set a new standard for athletes looking to take ownership of their futures. The repercussions would reshape the signature shoe business and later trickle into other areas. To Pyatt, Strahan and Shaquille O’Neal “were the first” to define the modern athlete production company movement, with the former building SMAC Entertainment alongside entertainment executive Constance Schwartz-Morini since 2010, as he transitioned from pro football player to daytime television talk show host. O’Neal, meanwhile, long has excelled at attracting opportunities and weaving them together, like becoming the president of Reebok’s basketball division in 2023 and then later selling a show to Netflix about revitalizing the brand through his production outfit, Jersey Legends. But much of the oxygen of the era belonged to James. In 2020, he formed the SpringHill Co. with his business partner Maverick Carter, raising $100 million from backers like Guggenheim Partners and Elisabeth Murdoch and consolidating three of his businesses — SpringHill Entertainment, Uninterrupted and the Robot Co. — into a new juggernaut. The joint enterprise had produced TV shows like Survivor’s Remorse , The Wall and The Shop , as well as such films as Space Jam: A New Legacy , Hustle and What’s My Name: Muhammad Ali . With the growing demands of streamers pushing Hollywood toward a TV production peak of 600 shows in 2022, investors poured into the space. The SpringHill Co. a year earlier had sold a minority interest to a group that included Nike, Fenway Sports Group and RedBird Capital Partners at a $725 million valuation. The enthusiasm extended beyond just athlete-led businesses, with Blackstone-backed Candle Media buying a majority stake in Reese Witherspoon’s media company, Hello Sunshine, for $900 million in 2021. Kevin Hart’s firm, Hartbeat, raised $100 million at a $650 million a year later. The proverbial gold rush didn’t last. The aftermath of the pandemic forced the industry to rethink its compensation models, and the bets investors were making on upside gave way to a more fundamentally sound approach. The strikes of 2023 only heightened that strain. “We used to have an economic climate where it was prioritizing growth as opposed to profit,” says Leonard Armato, the former CMO of Skechers who helped O’Neal launch his footwear brand and currently advises the No. 1 pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, AJ Dybantsa. “And that came sort of to a screeching halt around the time of WeWork.” Since then, media companies led by some of the biggest names in Hollywood, like Hart, Jordan Peele and J.J. Abrams, have undergone layoffs. Hello Sunshine reportedly missed its profit projections in 2023, and parent company Candle Media later restructured its business to cut costs . That same year, the Springhill Co. eliminated 10 roles, though it described the move as a pathway to hiring 24 new jobs. In 2024, Bloomberg reported that James’ enterprise had never turned a profit in its four-year life span, having lost a combined $45 million in 2022 and 2023. The SpringHill Co. did rev up its growth plans last year by merging with James Corden’s Fulwell 73, raising a war chest of $40 million from existing investors. For those soldiering on, the industry shift taught at least one valuable lesson. “Every project has to be undeniable,” says Erick Peyton, the co-founder of Curry’s Unanimous Media. Coco Gauff in Tennis Story Serve Fashion Tennis Story Serve Fashion & Tennis Courtesy of Tennis Channel A LITTLE HELP FROM FRIENDS Gauff has full creative control over iROC, but it’s not a day-to-day gig. She picks the projects, gives notes and, in some cases, appears on camera. On the two upcoming short films, Gauff estimates she put in about five to seven hours of work. That’s understandable, considering her tennis schedule. Yet it does stress the gravity of finding the right partner. Gauff chose Religion of Sports, which produced documentaries like Shut Up and Dribble , Man in the Arena and Simone Biles Rising . “I’m kind of creative, but not in the things of finding the right people, cameras, angles and the right person to do the interview,” she says. “Just like so many little things I’ve learned that it takes to create a short.” It’s a commonality among athlete-led production companies. James has Carter. Curry has Peyton. O’Neal has Michael Parris and Authentic Brands Group, which bought a share of his entire business interests in 2015. Strahan has Schwartz-Morini. And Manning has Jamie Horowitz. The duo behind Omaha Productions met in 2019 and formed the business a year later, rattling off hit shows like Peyton’s Places and Monday Night Football With Peyton and Eli . It didn’t take long for outside money to arrive. Peter Chernin’s North Road content studio invested $10 million at a $400 million valuation in 2023, and WTSL, the firm Pyatt would later join, entered Omaha Productions’ cap table two years later in a deal that valued the company at more than $750 million. That success starts at the top, according to Pyatt. “Peyton appeals to red states, and he appeals to blue states, which is very rare,” he says. “Then you have someone like Jamie, who can activate it with Peyton.” But while Omaha Productions or any other talent-led media business can launch off the popularity of its central figure, it must evolve to achieve long-term sustainability. “We used to call it the ‘What happens if that person gets hit by a bus?’ ” Pyatt says. Peyton and Eli Manning now only appear in about a quarter of Omaha Productions’ projects as opposed to more than 70 percent at the beginning. Some of Peyton Manning’s critical contributions to Netflix’s Quarterback docuseries came behind the camera, as the Pro Football Hall of Famer, who does briefly appear in the show, used his personal relationships to help the streamer secure “some of the marquee quarterbacks in the league,” according to Brandon Riegg, vp nonfiction series and sports at Netflix. Chasers-TOM BRADY Remembers EVERYTHING! episode Courtesy of Chasers Riegg, who has worked with James, Curry and O’Neal, in addition to Manning, adds that any production company has to be held to the same standard of developing and executing projects, even if a famous figurehead can lift some of the industry’s typical barriers to entry. When athletes do learn just how hard it is to operate in Hollywood, prolonged success in entertainment becomes a question of their “appetite, ambition and tolerance.” “This is a marathon; this isn’t a five-year thing,” Riegg says. “This is a business. It’s not like hitting the lottery. It’s like you have to do idea creation at a regular cadence.” To offset the challenges of Hollywood production, some media companies use branded content and commercial campaigns. Omaha Productions has shot commercials for the Mannings, as well as Baker Mayfield, Brock Purdy and Jordan Spieth. It also put together a show for the PGA of America starring Colin Jost that was paid for by T-Mobile. The branded content and commercial campaign vertical now accounts for roughly a quarter of Omaha Productions’ revenue, the highest percentage in the company’s brief history. Pyatt doesn’t see that changing, especially with industries like gambling upping their content spends. Gilad Haas, who co-founded production studio and marketing agency Shadow Lion with Brady, says his firm previously struck a deal with FanDuel that produced both a miniseries about the Boston Celtics 2024 championship and hundreds of man-on-the-street, social-style posts. The progression of production companies to full-fledged media businesses has also resulted in other moneymaking endeavors. The Shop , SpringHill Co.’s popular barbershop-style talk show, launched its own line of men’s grooming products. Unanimous Media’s Peyton says his firm wants to play a bigger role in financing projects and funneling creators and other non-traditional talents to larger studios. Many companies in the space are figuring out how to push into live events, if they haven’t already, as the AI age places a stronger emphasis on social gatherings and human connection. Gauff has her own designs on where she wants iROC to go, including producing a movie with a theatrical release. She’s got time, though. Her entertainment journey is starting much earlier than those of James, Curry or Manning. “I’m 22 years old, so there’s still going to be a lot of eyes on me when I’m playing,” she says. “Hopefully, by the time I retire, we build something that can sustain itself without me promoting it as an active player.” This story appears in The Hollywood Reporter’s September 2026 Sports issue .

title: Ellen Burstyn Talks Working Into 90s with Starring Role In Unexpected Love Story ‘Place To Be’; Pays Tribute To Gloria Steinem – Venice
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie LevelK Posts U.S. & Euro Sales Haul For Karlovy Vary Prizewinner ‘The Guest’ Casey Affleck’s ‘Company’ Earns 4.5-Minute Ovation At Venice World Premiere Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz Talk Playing Fictitious Arguing Couple In ‘Bunker’: “We Are Very Good At Creating Fiction & Reality” – Venice View All September 9, 2026 6:18am Murray Bartlett, Taika Waititi, Ellen Burstyn, Pamela Anderson and Director Kornél Mundruczó attend Place To Be Photocall at the Venice Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images Oscar-winning actress Ellen Burstyn addressed shifting attitudes to older woman in Hollywood ahead of the world premiere of Kornel Mundruzcó’s Place To Be , in which she co-stars opposite Taika Waititi , at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. The Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore and The Last Picture Show star revealed that she had started to question how long her career would last when she was in her 30s. “I was sure I’d be finished by 40. I didn’t think it would go on much longer than that. The fact that I’m 93 and still working is a miracle of some kind that I’ve attracted into my life somehow, and I’m totally amazed,” she said. I was sure I'd be finished by 40… The fact that I'm 93 and still working is a miracle" pic.twitter.com/mPPFzFuibF — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 9, 2026 She paid tribute to American feminist icon and founder of Ms. Magazine Gloria Steinem , who died at age 92 in early September . “Gloria Steinem is the one I’m thinking of… she started Ms. Magazine back then. What influenced me was Ms. Magazine,” she said, acting out with passion a line in Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore in which her character declared, “It’s my life. It’s not some man’s life that I’m helping him out with”. “That really was the way it was before the change, and thank God, thank God, the world changed and allowed women to be full human beings,” she continued with a mischievous smile to applause and laughter: “Was that a comment?” Burstyn stars in light-hearted road movie Place to Be opposite Waititi as an elderly widow who forges an unexpected deep connection with a middle-aged man she meets while travelling from Chicago to New York to return a lost racing pigeon to its owner. The chance meeting and connection helps them confront personal disappointments, to rediscover a sense of purpose and wonder at a time when both thought it was no longer possible in the stages of their respective lives. Burstyn and Waititi are joined in the cast by Murray Bartlett and Pamela Anderson who did not participate in the press conference. Kornel Mundruczó on wanting to create a love story for Ellen Burstyn with ‘Place to Be’ #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/FMfMkjEpzo — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 9, 2026 Mundruzcó told the press conference that he had first hit on the idea of developing a film for Burstyn after working with her briefly on his 2020 Oscar-nominated drama Pieces of a Woman. “I was totally fascinated by her, and I find I definitely wanted to make a movie for her, specifically for her. So, we started to develop it, and we watched all of her movies, although obviously we knew many of them,” said Mundruzcó, who directed the film from a screenplay by longtime collaborator Kata Weber. He said he quickly came to the conclusion that he wanted to create a love story for Burstyn. “That idea stayed all the way. How can I create a love story for her and other women at that age, in which the tone is kind of light and tender and kind of easy, but at the same time telling a very deep story.” Alongside accompanying Place to Be, Burstyn is also an honorary guest of the Venice Film Festival this year as a recipient of its Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement earlier this week .
