title: ‘Joie de Vivre. Notes, Thoughts, Words, Reflections, Faces, And Visions Concerning Bernardo Bertolucci And The Cinephilia Of The 20th Century That No Longer Exists’ Review: So Long, Maestro! – Venice Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews ‘The Spiral’ Review: Valeria Bruni Tedeschi Is The Devil In Disguise In Paolo Strippoli’s Fiendishly Fun Horror-Thriller – Venice Film Festival View All September 9, 2026 5:31am Luca Guadagnino's 'Joie de Vivre'. Venice Film Festival. Ostensibly a tribute to the late Bernardo Bertolucci (1941-2018), the one-time giant of Italian cinema whose star has waned somewhat in recent years, Luca Guadagnino ’s 426-minute docu-essay — nearly twice as long as Alex Gibney’s Musk — is the endurance test of this year’s Venice Film Festival. Surprisingly, however, watched in two sittings, it is less of an ordeal than it might appear, partly thanks to the director’s forthright views: from the outset, Guadagnino admits that certain titles in the late maestro’s filmography are just too rubbish to bother with. No Beseiged . No Little Buddha . No Stealing Beauty . Hooray! Related Stories Trailers 'Artificial' Teaser Trailer Shows Andrew Garfield As Sam Altman In Luca Guadagnino Film News Hanway Boards Luca Guadagnino's Bernardo Bertolucci Doc 'Joie De Vivre' There’s a roundabout quality to Joie de Vivre that works best in first half, which is much stronger than the second. Guadagnino’s approach is very personal, snooping around the director’s former home in Rome — Via della Lungara, 3, if you’re planning a pilgrimage — he seems to be actively trying to summon the late auteur’s ghost. The house is just as Bertolucci left it (and therefore just as his widow, Clare Peploe left it, before she died in the summer of 2021). Somehow, the house still feels alive with his presence, and one wonders if he might come barging into his study at any minute, furiously denying that the DVD copy of Promising Young Woman on display in any way belongs to him. Watch on Deadline Guadagnino comes at Bertolucci from many angles, even claiming to have fancied him as a younger man, but facts and figures don’t really seem to enter into his concept of biography. Bertolucci just bursts onto the screen, fully formed, with his first ‘official’ feature film, Before the Revolution (1964). Technically, this was actually his second film after 1962’s The Grim Reaper , but Guadagnino will return to that later. The director, it transpires, has pressganged a lot of his friends and peers to help him out, and to discuss Bertolucci’s first international breakout hit, he wheels out a big gun: Martin Scorsese. Scorsese was an early convert to Bertolucci’s reinvention of Italian cinema, having caught a screening of Before the Revolution at the New York Film Festival . “The new voice had arrived,” he says. “And I was there .” Scorsese leads an impressive cavalcade of directors that are as perceptive as they are surprising: Catherine Breillat, Alfonso Cuarón, David Cronenberg, Abderrahmane Sissako and… wait a minute, is that James Gray ? (It is.) Guadagnino’s next stop is The Conformist (1970) swiftly followed by Last Tango in Paris (1972), the one-two punch that set him up as a major player in world cinema. The former made him an arthouse deity, the second brought him notoriety and very nearly jail time. At this point, Guadagnino drafts in friends from the other side of the divide — critics and media commentators such as Jay Weissberg, Scott Foundas, Murielle Joudet, Oyku Sofuoglu and… wait a minute, is that “contrarian analyst” Armond White? (It is.) The debate about Last Tango is the chewy center of this otherwise freewheeling production, and this also where the film starts to find its feet. Last Tango is perhaps the perfect film to hold up to the light, since it has accrued many meanings in the half-century since release. Its sexual politics once seemed so liberal, and now they very much do not, a paradox Guadagnino digs into: Has the world changed or have we changed? He also has the director’s back, defending Bertolucci from misguided allegations that the film’s famous butter scene was somehow done for real and improvised without the actress’s knowledge. Nevertheless, there’s a fascinating discussion about the imbalance of power on set, and it’s probably just as well the interval occurs here. The second half begins with Bertolucci’s masterpiece, the self-explanatory 1900 (1976), a period epic featuring, together for the first time, Robert de Niro and Gerard Depardieu. There’s a scene of front-frontal male nudity (or rather there was in the festival cut) that’s still an eye-opener today, and, as special guest star Margot Robbie points out, “The greatest cocaine scene ever”. Which brings us swiftly on to La Luna (1976), the jaw-dropping — and thus almost impossible to see nowadays — story about an incestuous mother and her junkie son (“It approached heroin in a joyfully unexpected way”). Guadagnino spends a surprising amount of time on Bertolucci’s almost completely uninteresting last film, Me and You (2012), before barging into Jeremy Thomas’s house and talking all over him, as the latter tries to discuss his two films with Bertolucci, The Last Emperor (1987) and The Sheltering Sky (1990). The Dreamers (2003) gets no coverage at all — even though Bertolucci’s affection for the nouvelle vague is catalogued in the first half — and Guadagnino ends his film with a forlorn elegy for the past (“The cinema I grew up with is gone”). Which is true, but then people said that in 1927, when sound arrived. The ostensible subject matter of the film, Bernardo Bertolucci, often gets pushed aside by Guadagnino and co., even while the speakers onscreen complain that Bertolucci was often pushed aside as a filmmaker. (It happens; we know that.) Those digressions are interesting, for sure, but it makes for a frustrating experience; one minute Guadagnino is in Marty’s screening room, bowing at the altar, the next he’s being dragged round a desolate field, talking philosophy by a woman with a very stern expression and even more forbidding hair. Bertolucci was “taking reality and making it eternal”, says a talking head, in a film that takes reality and, at times, simply makes it seem eternal. Title: Joie de Vivre. full_text: Sep 9, 2026 5:11am PT Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Ellen Burstyn Was ‘Sure’ Her Career Would Be ‘Finished by 40’: ‘The Fact That I’m 93 and Working Is a Miracle’ 1 hour ago Casey Affleck and Nick Nolte Get Emotional as ‘Company’ Debuts in Venice; Ben Affleck Shows Up to Support 15 hours ago Elon Musk’s MAGA Shift, Self-Driving Cars, Myths About Mars and More Get Examined in New Documentary: 5 Biggest Revelations 21 hours ago See All Ellen Burstyn , an Oscar, Tony and Emmy winner for projects like “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore,” “Same Time, Next Year” and “Political Animals,” marvels that she’s still able to act as a nonagenarian. “When I was in my 30s and I thought about how long my career would last, I was sure I’d be finished by 40. I didn’t think it would go on much longer than that,” Burstyn said during a press conference for “ Place to Be ,” a quirky drama that debuts at Venice Film Festival on Wednesday. “The fact that I’m 93 and still working is a miracle of some kind that I’ve attracted into my life. I’m totally amazed, and at the same time, deeply grateful.” Related Stories The Next James Bond Has Been Picked, Says Gary Oldman, Whose 'Fingers Are Crossed' for 'Slow Horses' Co-Star Jack Lowden 'Star Wars' Heads to Imax 70mm for First Time With 'Starfighter' and 'A New Hope' 50th Anniversary Re-Release “Place to Be” stars Burstyn and Taika Waititi as a no-nonsense elderly woman and arrogant divorced man who form an unlikely friendship as she ventures from New York to Chicago to return a lost racing pigeon to its owner. Anderson skipped the press conference, which was attended by Burstyn, Waititi and Hungarian director Kornél Mundruczó. Burstyn has been using a walker because she recently took a fall, so Waititi gently helped her to her seat before the presser began. Popular on Variety Mundruczó said he developed the role of Brooke for Burstyn and noted that he rewatched much of her filmography as he wrote the part. “It was very beautiful to create a love story for her,” Mundruczó said of the platonic relationship between Burstyn and Waititi’s characters. Pigeons play a central role in “Place to Be,” and Mundruczó hopes the film will change the perception around a bird that he feels “get a bad rap.” “Pigeons are the losers of history. At the beginning, they were so important as messenger birds during war, and [they delivered] a ton of love stories,” Mundruczó said. “And then they became city rats. I found something very touching from these little birds.” Waititi swears he’s fond of pigeons, but he had one complaint about working with the birds. “They shit a lot. Every minute. And that’s a scientific fact,” Waititi said. “Physiologically, there’s something not right with them.” Producer Jomon Thomas revealed the filmmaking team had a meeting, where they considered using diapers for the 30 pigeons that appear in the movie. However, they decided against it because “it was tricky to take them off with visual effects.” Plus, Waititi chimed in, “nobody wants to take off a pigeon’s diaper…” “Place to Be” continues a career resurgence for Anderson. The former “Baywatch” star made her Broadway debut in 2022 as Roxie Hart in “Chicago” before earning some of the best reviews of her career for Gia Coppola’s drama “The Last Showgirl.” Anderson parlayed those raves into roles in “The Naked Gun,” “Rosebush Pruning” and “Place to Be.” Burstyn admits she was surprised at first when Pamela Anderson was cast as her daughter in “Place to Be.” “And then I met her and thought, ‘Oh, for sure, she could be my daughter.’ I felt immediately loving toward her,” Burstyn said. “She’s a wonderful person.” Burstyn is having a busy festival. The acting legend was in Venice for two movies (the other was Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Marilyn Monroe-inspired short “Flesh Impact”), and she received the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. At the ceremony for her career honor, Burstyn got emotional and broke down in tears as the audience greeted her with a standing ovation. “You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me. It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” Burstyn said on Monday at her Golden Lion tribute , prompting laughter from the crowd. “But this … it’s a lot.” ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review Loading comments... title: Channel 4 Confirms Plans To Cut More Than A Quarter Of Its Workforce
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Doctor Who’ Actor Noel Clarke Charged With Sexual Assault, Voyeurism & Exposure BBC Boss Matt Brittin Asked News Unit To Examine Jason Arday Coverage After Cambridge Professor’s Death ‘SNL UK’ Sets Amelia Dimoldenberg & Jamie Demetriou As Guest Hosts View All September 9, 2026 4:00am Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Channel 4/Getty Channel 4 has announced the deepest round of layoffs in its 43-year history. The British network, home to shows including The Great British Bake Off and Taskmaster , is planning to cut 340 jobs by the end of 2026, meaning its workforce will shrink by more than a quarter. Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra announced the layoffs on Wednesday after spending recent months overseeing a strategic review of the commercial broadcaster. She told employees that the redundancies — equivalent to 28% of Channel 4’s 1,276-strong workforce — will ensure that more of C4’s £1 billion ($1.3 billion) income is spent on screen. Related Stories News International Revenues Of $2.1B Boost British TV Makers, Census Finds, As Pact Warns BBC Must Avoid "Managed Decline" News Channel 4 "Deeply Saddened" By Death Of Employee Lolita Visa The scale of the cuts has shocked insiders and others close to Channel 4. One source described it as a “very bad” day for the British broadcaster. Watch on Deadline Channel 4 finds itself increasingly isolated in a world in which it is dwarfed in size by some of its production suppliers, rival networks, and digital giants like YouTube. The state-owned broadcaster is grappling with these forces at the same time as reckoning with ad market contraction and rising production costs. Dogra has designed a new organizational structure, aimed at reducing management layers, removing duplication, and simplifying decision-making. She is positioning the changes as “owning our future,” building on the work of her predecessor Alex Mahon in growing digital sales to 34% of Channel 4’s revenue. Channel 4’s announcement was, however, light on details about the new structure, including how it will impact commissioning and the network’s fledgling in-house production plans. A consultation process with staff will begin shortly. Channel 4 said further details will be announced about the plans in the coming months. Dogra said: “Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK. We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won’t, reach audiences others can’t, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations. “Today marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love. “The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation. Many talented people who have made an enormous contribution to Channel 4 will be leaving as a result. “These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4 that can invest a greater proportion of revenues into distinctive content, back British creativity and deliver impact for audiences long into the future.” Channel 4 chair Geoff Cooper added: “The proposals announced today are intended to secure Channel 4’s future as a trusted, independent British broadcaster. “By taking action now, it can build a more sustainable and resilient organisation, maximise investment in content and strengthen its ability to deliver public value for audiences, the creative industries and the UK for the years ahead.” Caroline Dinenage, chair of UK Parliament’s Culture, Media and Sport Committee, said the jobs cull was “deeply worrying” for Channel 4’s employees. “Channel 4 is a unique asset and must find ways to maintain independence and distinctiveness while capitalising on efficiencies and opportunities for collaboration,” she added. Channel 4’s job cuts follow similar redundancies at the BBC, which has committed to reducing its workforce by 10%, equating to around 2,000 layoffs. Channel 4’s last major round of redundancies came in 2024 when 200 roles were closed. Channel 4 cuts often spark conversations about the broadcaster’s executive pay, which reached record levels during Mahon’s tenure. Despite leaving Channel 4 in June 2025, Mahon’s total pay stood at £566,000, which is more than the BBC director-general earns in a year, despite running a considerably larger organization. PRIYA DOGRA EMAIL TO CHANNEL 4 STAFF: Thank you for joining the All Staff meeting today and I know many of you will now be in follow-up meetings with your ExCo member to understand what the announcement means for your role and your area. I appreciate this is a significant and unsettling moment for many of you, but particularly for those whose roles will be affected by the changes we are proposing. I want to be clear that we have not made these proposals lightly. They will affect many talented people who have contributed enormously to our success. Our intention is to support people through the process with care, respect and transparency. A lot of detail was covered in the All Staff, so I want to briefly summarise the key points. What I presented today is the first stage of our transformation strategy. This work is designed to help us prioritise investment in content, grow our impact and secure our long-term sustainability. We have proposed a new organisational design that will significantly decrease non-programming spend by reducing our overall headcount by approximately 340 roles, equivalent to 28% of our workforce, by the end of the year. These proposals are intended to create a simpler, more focused organisation and allow us to direct a greater proportion of our revenues towards distinctive British content. That investment is what allows us to have impact. But this transformation is not just about reducing costs. It is also about creating the platform for future growth, strengthening our revenues so that we can invest more in the content, creativity and public value that set Channel 4 apart well into the future. I explained why these changes are necessary: · The market around us has changed faster than expected. Audiences and advertisers are increasingly moving towards global platforms, while many of our competitors are becoming larger and better funded. Advertiser investment in UK television has fallen by more than £400 million since 2019 and is expected to decline further over the next five years. · At the same time, as a publicly owned, commercially funded broadcaster, we have fewer levers than many other organisations. We cannot simply cut profits to absorb financial pressure. Since 2019, while our revenue has remained broadly stable, our operating costs have increased by 25%. That means operating costs now account for a greater proportion of our revenue. In 2019, running Channel 4 cost us around 32p for every £1 of revenue we generated. Today that figure is around 40p. That means less of our revenue is available to invest in programmes, and as that declines, so does our ability to drive audience and revenue growth. That is not sustainable, and it is not what Channel 4 is here to do. · The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we are organised and how we operate. The proposed changes have been developed through a comprehensive review of roles, structures and ways of working across the organisation. They focus on reducing management layers, simplifying decision-making and removing duplication, so that we can build a leaner, more efficient operating model ready for the future. · Our overall goal is to spend more of our revenue on content, because content is how Channel 4 delivers impact. Our purpose matters more than ever: to tell stories others don’t, provide trusted news, represent the UK in all its diversity and remain a distinctive British public service broadcaster. By making difficult decisions today and reshaping our organisation now, we can create a more sustainable cost base so we can protect and strengthen that impact and secure Channel 4 as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for years to come. Work on our future strategic direction is well advanced and will be shared in the coming months. At its heart, the transformation’s theme is ‘owning our future’: reshaping how we reach audiences through distribution, partnerships and platforms; enabling greater investment in distinctive programmes that set Channel 4 apart; and ensuring resources are allocated to maximise long-term value, sustainability and public impact. Today’s announcement is the first stage of that transformation and is an important step towards delivering those goals. I know that the next few weeks are going to be very difficult, particularly for those directly impacted, but also for those of you whose teammates will be going through the process. We will continue to share updates throughout this process, and I will also be travelling to each of our offices in the coming weeks to meet with you, hear your views and answer questions – details will follow. I want to thank you in advance for the professionalism and care I know you will show to each other, and for everything you will continue to do for Channel 4. full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Netflix South Africa Slate Includes Latest ‘How To Ruin’, ‘Seriously Single’ & ‘Disaster Holiday’ Editions International Revenues Of $2.1B Boost British TV Makers, Census Finds, As Pact Warns BBC Must Avoid “Managed Decline” Prime Video Adds ‘The Test’ Season 4 & True-Crime Docs On Backpacker Poisonings And Killer Trio To Australian Slate View All September 9, 2026 3:30am 'Love is Blind South Africa', 'Seriously Single Too' 'Another Disaster Holiday, 'Tuiskoms' and 'How to Ruin Diwali: Meet the Parents' Netflix Netflix ‘s How to Ruin , Seriously Single and Disaster Holiday franchises are getting new editions as part of the streamer’s latest South African slate. Following the launch of Blood Legacy Season 2 on September 25, Netflix will debut Seriously Single Too , Another Disaster Holiday later this year, with Tuiskoms Season 2, Marked Season 2 and Meet the Khumalos 2 also in production. How to Ruin Diwali : Mee the Parents launches on October 30 and Dineo and Zothile ‘Solo Ntsizwa’ Langa have been confirmed as the hosts of Love is Blind: South Africa . Docuseries Stars & Vows: Anele and Buzza is another debuting in 2026. Related Stories News Netflix Orders 'Lonesome Dove' Series From Zoe Kazan & Jeb Stuart Based On Larry McMurtry's Novel News 'The Gentleman' Returns To 45% Audience Decline For Season 2 Debut On Netflix How to Ruin Diwali: Meet The Parents comes from Burnt Onion Productions in collaboration with producer, Jayan Moodley. The show takes an irreverent look at an interracial couple whose engagement brings together two very different families and cultures. Moodley’s comedy The Kandasamys drew on similar South African Indian family tropes. Watch on Deadline Per the synopsis, it follows overachieving perfectionist Mmabatho Nkomo meeting her fiance’s traditional Indian family for the first time as her desperate attempt to impress backfires when she accidentally exposes her future father-in-law’s secret affair. With Diwali only days away, Mmabatho must navigate unfamiliar cultural territory and reunite the family she has torn apart without causing even more chaos. Rosemary Zimu-Mnguni, Kyle Clark, Jailoshini Naidoo, Koobeshen Naidoo, Sonia Mbele, Meshack Mavuso, Luthando ‘BU’Mthembu, Denise Zimba and Ashish Gangapersad star. Another Disaster Holiday, directed by Rethabile Ramaphakela, sees Joseph Ngema (Kenneth Nkosi) preparing to become a dad again at 50 and fighting to prove he is still father of the year. Per the preamble, “Under the guise of a romantic Sun City babymoon with a heavily pregnant Nandi, Joseph sets out to crash his children’s holiday with his ex-wife Dora and the hot younger boyfriend stealing his thunder. Enter Kay Sibiya, who joins the returning star-studded cast as Dora’s new bae and Joseph’s newest competition. Naturally, disaster follows.” Seriously Single Too , also directed by Ramaphakela, sees Dineo (Fulu Mugovhani) and Noni (Tumi Morake) return, though their friendship may not last their latest trip. The pic follow what is supposed to be a wild bachelorette getaway in Cape Town for the now-estranged friends turn into a disastrous chain of events that leaves them on the brink. Also starring are Buntu Petse, Keke Mphuthi, Yonda Thomas and Thabiso Rammusi. Romcom series Tuiskoms ‘s second season sees Fleur (Amalia Uys) and Werner (Armand Aucamp) preparing for their wedding, before their carefully planned future takes an unexpected turn. Per the synopsis, “At the same time, a free-spirited woman with a complicated past returns to Wilderness after years away, hoping to reconnect with the family she left behind. Across the town, old wounds, new beginnings and unexpected connections reshape the lives of those who call it home.” Uys and Aucamp star alongside Kim Syster, Jane de Wet and Clint Brink. Netflix recently found a hit out of South Africa in the shape of The Polygamist, which generated over 24 million views in its first weeks, reached the Top 10 in 62 countries and ranked first in 22 countries. The streamer is this week celebrating ten years in the country, and has trotted out several stats backing its performance there. During a press showcase in Rosebank, Johannesburg, where Netflix executives, filmmakers and on-screen talent gathered to mark the occasion, the streamer claimed to have supported 8,000 jobs through partnerships with more than 30 local production companies. Its local originals have included Blood and Water , Silverton Siege , Fatal Seduction and most recent Umthetho , and have been filmed in 20 cities across eight provinces. Netflix claims to have offered more than 300 local titles in total over the past decade, including acquisitions. “Ten years ago, we set out to share South African stories and voices with the world and today, we are proud to strengthen our partnership with the local creative industry and continue creating exciting stories that will entertain our members in South Africa and around the world,” said Ben Amadasun, VP of Content for Netflix Middle East and Africa. “Our slate ahead keeps that ambition alive with the addition of established names alongside bold new production partners across genres from unscripted to thrillers, family dramas and comedy.” Netflix also teased a new scripted series from Shaka iLembe maker The Bomb Shelter Film Productions and a multi-title partnership with The River producer Tshedza Pictures for four scripted series.
